text.p: Pearson Chief Executive Marjorie Scardino vowed on Monday to double the value of the company and unveiled better than expected first half figures as a "first step" on the road to improved performance.

Pearson plc, owner of prized assets such as the Financial Times newspaper and Penguin books, said profit from continuing operations almost doubled to 65.5 million pounds ($106.8 million) in the first six months of 1997.
"These results represent the first step in our commitment to improve the company's performance," said Texan Scardino, who in January became the first woman to lead a top British company

She said in a statement that the goal was to double Pearson's value over the next five years and achieve annual double digit earnings per share growth. The company has a market capitalisation of about 4 billion pounds.
Finance Director John Makinson told Reuters the targets were "stretching" and added that the company "had nailed its colours firmly to the mast".
Initial market reaction to the announcement was positive, Pearson shares adding 23p to 689p by 0920 GMT.

"The results were ahead of our expectations and there was a very positive statement," said one media analyst. But he noted the rise after a recent underperformance had been capped by the lack of firm news on restructuring.

Makinson said Pearson was actively reviewing a diverse portfolio which includes a television production arm, the Madame Tussaud's waxwork exhibition and a 50 percent stake in London merchant bank Lazard Brothers.
He said decisions had already been made on the future of some businesses and added that Pearson portfolio would have a different look within five years.
Pearson reported a surge in first half profits at the Financial Times and a strong performance from Penguin as last December's acquisition of U.S. publisher Putnam Berkley was integrated swiftly.

"We expect further growth in group revenues and operating profits in the second half of the year, tempered by revenue investment in the Financial Times newspaper, Financial Times Information and Channel 5, as well as by the impact of sterling's strength," Scardino said.

Financial Times Information provides electronic financial information while Pearson has a large stake in Channel 5, the national commercial TV station launched in Britain in March. Pearson had start-up losses of 11.7 million pounds from Channel 5 in the first half.
Makinson said the strength of sterling, if maintained, would wipe some 20 million pounds off the pre-tax figure for the full year and cut sales revenues by 120 million.

Pearson increased its working capital by 48 million pounds to deal with accounting problems at its Penguin USA subsidiary. The company said it believed the 100 million pound provision taken in its 1996 accounts should cover the total losses.
Improper accounting at Penguin USA came to light earlier this year after going undetected since the early 1990s. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
